findings.title: A peer-declared 32-bit length sizes a byte[] before any payload is read, committing up to ~2 GiB from 4 bytes on the wire

location.component: ValueReader.readBytes(DataInputStream), reached from readLongstr(), readTable() and readFieldValue() cases 'S' and 'x'

findings.evidence: Lines 86-89: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` then `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]; in.readFully(buffer); }`. The guard on line 87 is a cast-safety test, not a limit: it only stops the narrowing to int from wrapping and admits every value below 2147483647. The array on line 88 exists before line 89 ever asks the stream for a byte. Reproduced locally against an unmodified copy of this file, compiled with JDK 17 and run with -Xmx64m: (a) 5 bytes on the wire - field-value type 'x' plus the four length bytes 0x40000000 and no payload - produced `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` inside readFieldValue; (b) the public API path, `new ValueReader(in).readLongstr()` over exactly 4 bytes declaring 2147483632 and no payload, produced the same. Both times the stream contained no data at all beyond the length prefix, which is what shows the allocation precedes the read.
findings.impact: Any peer that supplies the byte stream this class decodes can make the client JVM commit up to about 2 GiB of heap per declared value while sending only four bytes - an amplification of roughly 5x10^8. A single frame carrying a field table can repeat the trick per field. The result is OutOfMemoryError, which in a JVM is not confined to the connection that caused it: it lands on whichever thread allocates next and takes down unrelated work in the same process, including other tenants of that application.
findings.preconditions: The client decodes a frame from a peer it does not control: a malicious or compromised broker, an attacker-operated endpoint the application was pointed at, or an active network position on a connection that is not using TLS. No credential is needed by the attacker, and no non-default client setting is required.
findings.recommendation: Bound the declared length against something the peer does not choose, before the array is created. The negotiated frame maximum is the natural bound, so pass it into ValueReader (constructor parameter, as the class is already constructed per stream) and reject a contentLength above it with MalformedFrameException; where no negotiated value is available, `min(declared, bytes actually remaining in the frame)` is the fallback, and a hard ceiling constant is the floor of the design. A growing structure - reading in capped chunks into a ByteArrayOutputStream - removes the class entirely at the cost of a copy. Add a regression test that feeds a length prefix with no payload and asserts a MalformedFrameException rather than an allocation; the test must fail without the patch.

triage.reason: No outer control can rule this out, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of what the missing files contain: the allocation on line 88 happens before the read on line 89, so a layer that bounds how many bytes are DELIVERED (a frame-size check, a truncating stream) cannot bound how many bytes are COMMITTED. Only a check on contentLength itself, inside readBytes, would qualify, and lines 86-89 contain none.
The value is `unsignedExtend(in.readInt())` on line 86 - four bytes taken straight off the stream with no allowlist, constant or prior validation between the wire and the allocation.

Two boundaries are crossed, either of which is sufficient. Remote peer to client process: this is the AMQP decoder and the bytes are the peer's. Library to consumer (local-app.md §0, fifth bullet): `public class ValueReader` with a `public ValueReader(DataInputStream)` and `public final LongString readLongstr()` is an exported surface, and the reproduction used exactly that surface.

findings.limits: This establishes that the allocation is unbounded and that it is reachable through the class's own public API. It does not establish which frames of the AMQP handshake reach it, because the callers - Frame, AMQConnection, the generated AMQImpl - are not in the target. WEB-26 notes that this family has its highest yield before authentication, and in AMQP 0-9-1 the peer's server-properties field table is decoded during connection negotiation; that specific pre-authentication path is a reasonable reading of the protocol, not something observed in files in scope, and the finding does not rest on it. Nor does this audit assert anything about whether upstream fixed, regressed or never had this bound: no VCS history and no advisory source was available.

findings.title: Mutual recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray carries no depth counter: 43 KB of nested arrays overflows the stack

location.component: readFieldValue (line 158) <-> readTable (line 139, case 'F') and readArray (line 237, case 'A')

findings.evidence: None of the three signatures carries a depth parameter: `static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)`, `private static Map<String,Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)`, `private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)`. Case 'F' (line 181) and case 'A' (line 184) call back into the pair unconditionally, and each nesting level costs the attacker 5 bytes for an array ('A' plus a 4-byte length) or 6 for a table. Reproduced locally against an unmodified copy of this file, JDK 17, default thread stack: depth 50000 (250000 bytes) raised StackOverflowError, and a binary search over the depth put the smallest overflowing input at depth 8593, i.e. 42965 bytes - comfortably inside a single frame at the AMQP default frame maximum of 131072 bytes, so no oversized frame is needed.
findings.impact: A peer can raise StackOverflowError inside the client's frame-decoding path with a single well-formed frame of about 43 KB. StackOverflowError is an Error, not the IOException the decoder's callers are written around, so it unwinds past the protocol error handling: the connection is left in an undefined state and the thread that was decoding dies. Repeatable at will and for a few kilobytes per attempt.
findings.preconditions: Same as F-001: the client decodes a frame from a peer it does not control. The payload is structurally valid AMQP - a legal field-array nested in a legal field-array - so nothing malformed has to get past an earlier check.
findings.recommendation: Thread a depth argument through readFieldValue, readTable and readArray, cap it at a small constant (the protocol has no legitimate use for deep nesting; single digits are generous), and throw MalformedFrameException on exceedance. Keep the public entry points on the current signatures and delegate to depth-carrying private overloads so the API does not change. Regression test: a field value nested past the cap must raise MalformedFrameException, and the same test at cap-minus-one must still parse.

triage.reason: The only bound in the code is the TruncatedInputStream wrapper built on lines 146-147 and 241-242, and it bounds bytes, not depth. Depth costs 5 bytes per level, so a byte bound at the AMQP default of 131072 still permits about 26000 levels while the measured overflow arrives at 8593. A byte limit therefore cannot be the missing control.
The type discriminator that drives the recursion is `in.readUnsignedByte()` on line 161 and the nested lengths are read from the same stream - all peer-chosen.
Same two crossings as F-001: remote peer to client process, and library to consumer through the public readTable() on line 252.

findings.limits: The reproduction needed TruncatedInputStream, which is NOT in the target; the audit wrote a minimal bounded FilterInputStream stub for it. findings.title: The public decoder is correct only over a fully buffered stream: table and array loops terminate on available()

location.component: readTable (line 148) and readArray (line 244); public constructor ValueReader(DataInputStream) at line 57

findings.evidence: `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` on line 148 and `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` on line 244 use the loop terminator that InputStream documents as an estimate of what can be read without blocking, not as a count of what remains. The class's public constructor at line 57 accepts any DataInputStream, its class javadoc says only 'Helper class to read AMQP wire-protocol encoded values', and nothing in the file states the precondition that the stream must already hold the whole frame. Handed a socket-backed stream, a table whose bytes have not all arrived terminates early and returns a partial Map with no error, and the caller resumes decoding at an offset that is now wrong.
findings.impact: A consumer that builds a ValueReader over a network stream - which the exported signature invites - gets silently truncated tables instead of an exception, and a decoder desynchronised against the wire. Inside the library's own shipped call path the streams are frame-backed and the defect does not fire, so what this grants an attacker today is nothing; the exposure is the default the next consumer inherits.
findings.preconditions: A consumer of the published artifact constructs ValueReader over a stream that is not fully buffered, following only the exported signature.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive the loop bound from available(). Track the declared table or array length explicitly and read exactly that many bytes, treating a short read as MalformedFrameException. Failing that, make the precondition part of the contract: take the frame payload as a byte[] or a ByteArrayInputStream in the public constructor, or document and enforce it.

triage.reason: The compensating behaviour would live in TruncatedInputStream.available(), which is not in the target and was not read. If it returned the remaining limit without consulting the underlying stream, the truncation would not occur. This UNKNOWN is why the finding is not reported as anything stronger than hardening; per FP-08 the absence of that file is not a pass.
The stream contents are peer-supplied; only the choice of stream belongs to the consumer.

findings.title: Table keys are decoded with lenient UTF-8, so distinct wire names collapse onto one String key

location.component: readShortstr, used for every field name in readTable

findings.evidence: Line 70 is `return new String(b, "utf-8");`, the constructor that replaces malformed input with U+FFFD instead of rejecting it. Reproduced through the public readTable(): a table containing two entries whose names on the wire are the byte pairs C0 80 and C1 80 - two different, both invalid, sequences - produced a single map entry, because both names decoded to the same two replacement characters.
findings.impact: The decoder is not injective from wire bytes to table keys: an attacker who controls the bytes of a field name can produce a key that is indistinguishable, after decoding, from a different name. Nothing in scope makes a decision on a header, so this grants nothing on its own; it is the precondition that a smuggling differential would need.
findings.preconditions: A peer supplies a field table whose names contain invalid UTF-8. No client configuration is involved.
findings.recommendation: Decode with a CharsetDecoder configured to REPORT on malformed and unmappable input and turn the CharacterCodingException into MalformedFrameException, so an undecodable name is a protocol error rather than a silent rename. Use StandardCharsets.UTF_8 rather than the string literal while doing so, which also removes the unnecessary checked-exception surface of the literal-charset constructor.

findings.title: Duplicate field names in a table are resolved first-wins and the later value is dropped without error
findings.evidence: Lines 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` - the second and later occurrences of a name are read off the wire, decoded into an Object, and then discarded silently. findings.impact: Where two AMQP implementations disagree on which duplicate wins - first, last, or reject - the same bytes carry two meanings. An application that routes or authorizes on a message header would then see a different value from whatever component validated it. No such second implementation was examined, so nothing is granted here today.

findings.recommendation: Reject a repeated field name with MalformedFrameException rather than silently keeping one of the two. If compatibility forbids rejecting, state the resolution rule in the javadoc so a consumer can reason about it, and keep it identical to the broker's.

triage.reason: Both the duplicate names and their values come from the peer's frame, read on lines 149-150.

findings.title: Source code for the published jar is generated from an unpinned checkout outside the repository, and a file two levels up can repoint it

location.component: groovy-maven-plugin execution `generate-amqp-sources` (plugin at line 597, script at line 621), properties `deps.dir` / `codegen.dir` (lines 110-111), and profile `in-umbrella` (line 133)

findings.evidence: At `generate-sources`, org.codehaus.gmaven:groovy-maven-plugin runs `${groovy-scripts.dir}/generate_amqp_sources.groovy`, which the pom's own comment describes as a proxy for executing the Python script `${basedir}/codegen.py` against the spec `${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json`. `codegen.dir` defaults to `${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen` and `deps.dir` to `${basedir}/deps` - a checkout that the pom never pins by commit, tag or digest and never verifies by hash or signature. build-helper-maven-plugin then adds `${project.build.directory}/generated-sources/src/main/java` as a compile source root, so AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java, produced from that unverified input, are compiled into the published artifact. Separately, the profile `in-umbrella` is activated by `<file><exists>../../UMBRELLA.md</exists></file>` and rewrites `deps.dir` to `${basedir}/..`: the mere presence of a file two directories above the repository silently changes where the build's source of truth comes from.
findings.impact: Whoever can write to the codegen checkout - or place an UMBRELLA.md and a matching tree above the build directory, which is the shape of a hostile working directory rather than a remote attack - chooses Java source that ships inside com.rabbitmq:amqp-client. Nothing in the build would flag it: there is no digest to compare and no signature to fail.
findings.preconditions: Write access to the build machine's `deps/` directory or to the parent-of-parent directory of the checkout, or control of the codegen repository or the transport used to clone it. On a developer machine that is the developer; on a shared or automated builder it is anyone with the same reach.
findings.recommendation: Pin the codegen input: vendor the AMQP spec JSON into the repository, or record the expected commit and verify it (or a sha256 of the spec file) before generate-sources runs, failing the build on mismatch. Drop the filesystem-triggered `in-umbrella` activation in favour of an explicit `-P` profile or property, so the build's inputs never change because of a file nobody in the repository controls.

triage.reason: A control could exist outside this file - a documented clone procedure in the README, a pinned submodule, a CI step that fetches a fixed revision. None of those artifacts is in the target and none was provided, so per FP-08's doctrine this is UNKNOWN and not a pass. It is also why the finding is hardening rather than probable.

The path is in what ships. The groovy execution is bound to the `generate-sources` phase of the default build with no profile guard, and build-helper adds the generated directory to the compile source root unconditionally, so the output is inside the released jar rather than in a developer-only side path.

findings.limits: codegen.py, generate_amqp_sources.groovy and the deps/ directory are not in the target, so what the script actually does with the spec was not read - only that the pom hands it an unverified input and compiles the result. No claim is made that any real build has been tampered with.
